title: Work-class underwater vehicles powered by the ocean

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an underwater vehicle that gathers energy from its ocean environment and uses it to sustain useful work without a tender supplying energy. Its capability would extend beyond persistent observation to long transits, controlled hovering and repeated mechanical intervention, with enough sustained and peak power for specified tools and tasks. Ocean temperature differences, waves or another ambient resource could supply energy, but each approach would need its own demonstrated resource and energy balance. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Existing environmental propulsion illustrates part of the idea. The thermal Slocum prototype used differences between warmer surface water and colder deep water to drive buoyancy changes; wings converted vertical movement into horizontal travel. The Wave Glider uses surface waves for propulsion and solar-charged batteries for onboard electrical systems. These examples demonstrate ways to obtain propulsion from the environment, but the supplied accounts do not demonstrate sustained underwater transit, hovering and repeated work at kilowatt-class mechanical output.

As a system-level synthesis, the central advance would combine energy capture, conversion, storage, propulsion, tooling, control and durability in a vehicle that remains useful throughout a long mission. A new conversion principle could help, but the evidence does not establish that one is necessary: improved integration of existing principles could potentially suffice. The defining outcome is sustained underwater working capability supported by ambient energy.

significance.text: Conventional work-class equipment provides a demanding power reference. The supplied review of the 2024 Ocean Robotics Planet buyers guide identifies work-class ROV ratings in the tens to hundreds of kilowatts, including a 150 kW maximum rating for the Perry XLX EVO II and a 175 kW electric rating for the Oceaneering eNOVUS. These specifications illustrate the scale associated with powered intervention. They are equipment ratings, however, and do not establish actual continuous consumption, ship-fed energy delivery or mechanical power delivered to tools.

The proposed revolutionary consequence is persistent intervention with much less dependence on energy replenishment and support vessels wherever the selected resource and operating conditions suffice. A vehicle able to travel, hold position and repeatedly perform useful work could remain available between tasks instead of ending a mission when its carried energy is exhausted. As a conditional downstream possibility, that persistence could support repeated inspection, maintenance or instrument servicing over long periods. These are consequences inferred from the proposed capability, not demonstrated outcomes of the cited glider trials.

The sustained-flight analogy captures the ambition of maintaining a useful mobile presence through environmental energy. It is an interpretive analogy, not an established historical equivalence or a prediction of feasibility. A one-year demonstration would establish operation for that tested year; it would not establish years of service, unlimited range, maintenance-free operation or reliable autonomy in every setting. Energy harvesting would also leave hydrostatic-pressure constraints and high-speed propulsion challenges to be solved separately.

Resource availability places a fundamental boundary on the impact. The documented thermal approach depends on access to warmer and colder water, so insufficient accessible temperature differences would constrain it. This limitation cannot be generalized to wave energy or every other ambient resource. The supplied material does not establish a geographic map of suitable thermal conditions, including the earlier claims about much of the deep ocean or high latitudes in winter.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability in this proposal is a durable ambient-energy vehicle system that sustains underwater working power throughout a long mission. The supplied examples establish buoyancy-driven thermal gliding and wave-driven propulsion, but do not demonstrate sustained kilowatt-class mechanical output for transit, hovering and repeated intervention. They provide a concrete starting point for the challenge without establishing a universal power ceiling for all known converters or proving that no qualifying system exists.

Engineering synthesis: the vehicle must collect enough usable energy under its actual operating conditions while meeting both average demand and short periods of high demand. Storage and power management would need to bridge resource fluctuations and tool loads. Capture hardware must also fit a useful vehicle: added drag, mass or operational constraints could consume the benefit of harvesting more energy. The required advance is therefore an adequate whole-mission energy balance with useful task performance, rather than a converter output measurement alone.

Durability is a separate barrier from energy availability. WHOI reports that, in its Wave Glider experience, biofouling and mechanical wear limit practical endurance to a few months despite theoretically unlimited energy endurance. A proposed long-lived working vehicle would need to retain energy-capture performance and mechanical operability despite those effects. This is an experience-based limitation of the documented platform, not a universal lifetime law for every ambient-powered vehicle.

Engineering synthesis: energy persistence must be matched by reliable control, navigation, tooling and fault recovery. A vehicle could harvest sufficient energy yet fail to hold position for a task, suffer a tool failure or require frequent human intervention. Demonstrating these capabilities together is essential to the proposed work-class role. Neither successful harvesting nor a kilowatt-class average alone establishes equivalence to the much higher-rated conventional ROVs in the supplied guide.

current_state.text: WHOI's Oceanus account, dated 25 September 2008, describes a prototype thermal glider launched in December 2007 and recovered in April 2008 after traveling more than 1,600 nautical miles, approximately 3,000 km. The roughly four-month trial demonstrated ocean-heat-powered propulsion. Alkaline batteries powered the electronics and were then the principal endurance limit, so the trial did not demonstrate a vehicle running all systems solely on ambient ocean energy. The supplied review found no six-month endurance projection in the full article.

The research notes attribute design goals of 40,000 km and five years to a July 2000 Webb Research report on a thermocline-powered glider. No captured document or extracted text for that DTIC URL was available to the supplied review, so the report's identity, numerical goals and context remain unverified here. These figures are retained as an unresolved historical attribution and must not be treated as achieved distance or endurance.

WHOI's Slocum platform description reports buoyancy-pump gliders moving horizontally below 1 knot, with endurance of weeks to months and GPS and Iridium satellite communications equipment. This supports the slow, persistent observation comparison. The supplied review found no explicit statement on that page establishing electrical propulsion power or surfacing specifically for GPS, so those details are not asserted from it.

WHOI's Wave Glider description reports wave-powered propulsion at 1–3 knots and solar-charged batteries supplying onboard electrical systems. It distinguishes theoretically unlimited energy endurance from practical endurance of a few months in WHOI's experience because of biofouling and mechanical wear. The platform combines a surface float with a tethered submerged component; it demonstrates persistent environmental observation, rather than the tender-free underwater working capability proposed here. Its speed also shows why the below-one-knot description should be restricted to the cited Slocum gliders.

The supplied review retained intact manufacturer entries from the 2024 buyers guide for the 150 kW maximum-rated Perry XLX EVO II and the 175 kW electric-rated eNOVUS. The guide extraction was partial and truncated on supplied PDF page 56, but the cited entries occurred before that truncation. They support a comparison of equipment power ratings, not a measured gap between glider mechanical output and ROV continuous working power.

Taken together, these records establish historical ambient-powered propulsion, persistent observation and practical endurance constraints. They do not quantify the earlier characterization of watt-scale locomotion or establish whether a vehicle meeting the proposed working capability existed as of 1 November 2026. The supplied review had an empty bounded search record, so field-wide freshness remains unassessed. That limitation does not invalidate the dated demonstrations.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a vehicle without a tender completes at least one year of long transits and repeated mechanical or high-power survey tasks, using ambient ocean energy as its sole net energy source, and is recovered still operable. One year is a proposed threshold for this record, not a published consensus standard. Success would establish the tested duration and mission capability; it would not demonstrate multi-year service or literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Yearlong tenderless underwater work uses solely ambient ocean energy

completion_criteria.text: The demonstration should specify transit distance, task outputs, task duty cycles, hovering requirements and the environmental resource conditions encountered. Mechanical output averaged over the full mission should be in the kilowatt class, with enough peak power and control to perform the declared tasks. Electrical survey consumption should be measured separately: high instrument demand cannot substitute for evidence of delivered mechanical work. Meeting the proposed average-power threshold would not by itself establish equivalence to conventional work-class ROVs.
completion_criteria.label: Kilowatt-class mission-average mechanical output supports declared underwater tasks

completion_criteria.text: An auditable energy balance should report initial and final stored energy, all external energy inputs, harvested energy and the principal loads. The accounting should show that depletion of initially carried energy did not sustain the claimed mission capability. Permitted maintenance and human intervention should be defined in advance and disclosed, including any cleaning, repairs, replacement parts or outside assistance. Recovery in an operable condition should include functional checks of propulsion, harvesting and the equipment used for the demonstrated tasks.
completion_criteria.label: Auditable energy accounting shows carried-energy depletion did not sustain capability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements include accessible mission logs, calibrated power and task measurements, and repeat demonstrations sufficient for others to assess the result. Testing across declared resource conditions should establish an operating envelope and identify conditions requiring reduced activity or mission termination. A finite set of successful missions would demonstrate breadth within those conditions. Sensor-only gliding or wave-propelled surface observation would not satisfy the proposed underwater working scope.
completion_criteria.label: Repeat underwater working missions establish a reproducible operating envelope

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MNE-07, Persistent abyssal work, with depth no longer the cost driver, is the closest complementary concept. MNE-08 addresses the energy source and endurance of useful underwater work; MNE-07 addresses the burden associated with operating at great depth. Ambient energy would not by itself establish pressure tolerance or reduce depth-related costs, and an economical abyssal work system could still depend on carried or externally supplied energy. The supplied roster provides no further MNE-07 evidence for a stronger comparison.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-05, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing, and MNE-06, Through-seawater links beyond the acoustic range–rate ceiling, concern capabilities that could complement long unattended missions. Persistent energy does not itself provide basin-scale position fixes or high-capacity underwater communications. Conversely, better positioning and links do not supply propulsion or tool energy. MNE-10, Coherent observability of the deep-ocean volume, concerns an observational outcome that persistent vehicles might help support, but a working vehicle alone would not establish coherent coverage of the ocean volume.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-01, Ship-scale collapse of turbulent skin friction, could reduce energy demand, while MNE-03, Seawater magnetohydrodynamic propulsion at propeller-class efficiency, concerns a propulsion method and its efficiency. Both could interact with a vehicle's energy budget, but MNE-08 concerns obtaining sustained energy from the environment and converting it into useful underwater work. Neither reduced friction nor efficient propulsion alone establishes that ambient supply can meet mission demand.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-02, Merchant ships freed from the displacement-hull speed barrier, addresses surface-ship speed, and MNE-04, Controlled, sustained supercavitating travel, addresses a distinct underwater travel regime. MNE-08 does not imply either speed breakthrough. Its proposed combination of endurance, hovering and repeated work must be assessed through its own energy and task requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-09, Storm-stable floating land in the open ocean, concerns persistent surface infrastructure. Such infrastructure could conceivably support underwater operations, but relying on it for supplied energy would not demonstrate the tender-free ambient-powered vehicle proposed here. Producing fuel aboard a surface ship is likewise a separate energy architecture. These distinctions preserve the vehicle concept without assuming details absent from the supplied roster.

change_log.change: Preserved MNE-08 and its title while defining the innovation as an integrated ambient-powered underwater working system.
change_log.reason: The useful concept survives corrections to individual supporting assertions; its achievement is not established by the supplied evidence.

change_log.change: Replaced universal claims about known converters and a required new conversion principle with a gap limited to the documented examples.
change_log.reason: The evidence establishes environmental propulsion in those examples, not a field-wide power ceiling or the necessity of a new physical principle.

change_log.change: Separated ocean-powered propulsion from battery-powered electronics in the December 2007–April 2008 thermal-glider trial, retaining the distance of more than 1,600 nautical miles.
change_log.reason: The trial did not demonstrate ambient energy supplying every onboard system.

change_log.change: Removed the asserted six-month projection and retained the reported 40,000 km and five-year goals only as an unverified historical attribution.
change_log.reason: The supplied full Oceanus text lacked the projection, and the DTIC report had no captured artifact for verification.

change_log.change: Restricted the below-one-knot speed to Slocum gliders, retained the Wave Glider's 1–3 knots, and qualified fouling and wear limits as WHOI's experience.
change_log.reason: The platforms have different propulsion architectures and speeds, and the reported practical lifetime is not a universal limit.

change_log.change: Replaced continuous ship-fed power and watt-scale locomotion claims with supported equipment ratings and an unquantified working-power gap.
change_log.reason: The guide provides ratings, while the supplied glider accounts do not establish measured mechanical output. Partial guide extraction still preserved the cited entries.

change_log.change: Qualified the sustained-flight analogy, multi-year ambition and resource limitations.
change_log.reason: The analogy is an impact judgment; a one-year test cannot establish years of service, and thermal-gradient constraints cannot be generalized to all ambient resources.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to include full-mission mechanical-power averaging, peak task performance, separate survey loads, stored-energy accounting, maintenance disclosure and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These definitions make the proposal assessable without presenting its thresholds as standards or equating kilowatt-class averages with conventional ROV capability.

change_log.change: Added roster-based distinctions for every other supplied concept and retained the absence of a current field-wide assessment.
change_log.reason: Related advances should remain separate, and the empty freshness record cannot establish whether the proposed capability remains unachieved.

unresolved_issues: Whether any vehicle met the proposed ambient-powered underwater working capability as of 1 November 2026 remains unassessed; the supplied review contains no bounded search results.
The cited DTIC report's identity, date, numerical design goals and context require verification from the document. Missing access does not establish that the attribution is false.
The supplied evidence does not quantify mechanical output for the glider examples or actual continuous consumption and delivered mechanical power for the cited ROVs.
The vehicle architecture, ambient resource, conversion and storage performance, and feasible operating envelope remain unspecified.
The proposed test still needs numerical transit distances, defined task outputs and duty cycles, maintenance allowances, measurement tolerances and a repeat-demonstration plan.
The roster supplies titles rather than supporting records for related concepts, so their relationships are conceptual distinctions rather than validated technical comparisons.

brief.title: Underwater robots powered by the ocean
possible: Ocean researchers and maintenance crews could leave a robot underwater to travel long distances, hold position and repeatedly use tools without a support vessel supplying energy. It would gather energy from its surroundings to keep working.
The robot could remain available between jobs, returning to inspect equipment, perform maintenance or service instruments instead of ending its mission when its stored energy runs out.
why: This would reduce dependence on energy replenishment and support vessels for underwater work. Persistent robots could make repeated inspection and maintenance possible over long periods.

sources.who: Teledyne Webb Research and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution
sources.showed: Slocum gliders change their buoyancy, or tendency to float, to rise and sink. Wings turn that movement into slow forward travel, allowing observation missions lasting weeks to months.
sources.quote: Slocum gliders are capable of moving horizontally at slow speeds (< 1 knot), and they can stay at sea for weeks to months at a time.
sources.cited_for: Slow underwater travel can support long observation missions.
sources.not_established: This platform description does not demonstrate ocean-powered tool use or sustained hovering.

sources.who: Oceaneering and the makers of the Perry XLX EVO II
sources.showed: Manufacturer specifications describe powerful underwater work vehicles. The Perry XLX EVO II has a maximum rating of 150 kilowatts, a measure of power.
sources.cited_for: Conventional underwater work vehicles provide a demanding power comparison.
sources.not_established: Equipment ratings do not measure continuous energy use or mechanical power delivered to tools.

sources.who: Webb Research, WHOI and the University of the Virgin Islands
sources.showed: A prototype used the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water to propel itself for roughly four months. Batteries powered its electronics.
sources.quote: Researchers have successfully flown the first thermal glider through the ocean—a robotic vehicle that can propel itself for several months across thousands of miles, using only heat energy from the ocean.
sources.cited_for: Ocean heat has powered sustained underwater travel.
sources.not_established: The trial did not demonstrate all systems running on environmental energy, hovering or repeated mechanical work.

sources.showed: This is a design report about a glider powered by differences in ocean temperature.
sources.cited_for: The report concerns a proposed ocean-heat-powered glider.
sources.not_established: Design goals do not establish achieved endurance or underwater working capability.

sources.who: Liquid Robotics and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution
sources.showed: Wave Gliders use waves for propulsion and solar-charged batteries for onboard systems. WHOI reports that marine growth and mechanical wear limit practical endurance to a few months.
sources.quote: We no longer use wave gliders for research on baleen whales that make low-frequency calls because of these issues.
sources.cited_for: Environmental energy can sustain observation, while wear and marine growth still limit endurance.
sources.not_established: A surface float with a tethered submerged component does not demonstrate independent underwater travel and tool use.

shown: A team from Webb Research, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and the University of the Virgin Islands demonstrated roughly four months of ocean-heat-powered propulsion. The glider still needed batteries for its electronics.

Liquid Robotics’ Wave Glider combines wave-powered travel with solar-powered onboard systems. WHOI’s experience shows that marine growth and mechanical wear can end missions even when energy remains available.
missing: A complete vehicle must gather enough energy for travel, hovering and repeated tool use throughout a long mission.
Energy storage must bridge fluctuations in the ocean resource and brief periods of high tool demand.
Energy collection and moving parts must keep working despite marine growth and wear.
Navigation, tool control and recovery from faults must remain reliable throughout the mission.

milestones.label: A year of underwater work powered by the ocean
milestones.explanation: A vehicle would have to complete a year of long journeys and repeated mechanical or demanding survey tasks, using only environmental energy and returning operable. This would establish sustained work without an energy-supplying vessel.

milestones.label: Sustained mechanical power for declared tasks
milestones.explanation: Mechanical output must average in the kilowatt range, a measure of power, across the mission, with sufficient peaks and control for declared travel, hovering and tasks. This would establish useful work beyond powering instruments.

milestones.label: Energy accounting proves the ocean sustained the work
milestones.explanation: An energy balance must show that stored-energy depletion did not sustain the work, with assistance disclosed under predefined rules and equipment functional at recovery. This would establish what powered the mission and what survived.

milestones.label: Repeated missions establish where the vehicle can work
milestones.explanation: Repeat underwater working missions must provide accessible logs and calibrated power and task measurements across declared resource conditions. This would establish reproducibility and the conditions requiring reduced work or mission termination.

uncertain: The vehicle design, energy source and achievable working conditions remain unspecified.
The proposed yearlong test is a chosen threshold; task demands, maintenance allowances and measurement tolerances still need definitions.
It remains unclear how much mechanical power the demonstrated gliders deliver compared with conventional underwater work vehicles.
